content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper works on the explanation of text classification models by assigning importance scores to input words. Based on the observation that estimating Shapley values requires many samples (on the order of hundreds to thousands) to get stable estimates especially for long inputs, this paper proposes to learn a predictor that directly predicts these values in a supervised way. While training is expensive, the cost at test time is much cheaper than sampling-based methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Nice insights that sampling-based estimator is unstable especially for long inputs.
2. Much cheaper way of estimating Shapley values than the sampling baseline and works decently.
3. The predictor is stable across training time randomness.

Weaknesses:
1. While stability is important, faithfulness is also important in model explanation. The predicted values do not correlate very well with the "ground truth" (estimated values using a large number of samples): for example, on MNLI the Spearman correlation is 0.42 which is in between taking 200 to 2000 samples.
2. The sample-based baseline allows trading-off accuracy with compute, but the proposed method cannot (at least not in the current paper). I think this work would be stronger if the proposed predictor can be used for guided importance sampling and show that its performance can improve by using more compute.
3. As also mentioned by the authors, the proposed approach can be potentially improved by using a ranking loss, as evidenced in Table 3: the proposed method does really well in terms of MSE, which is what it trained for, so training with ranking loss might get better Spearman correlation values.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This work is clear, well-written, and original.
content.summary_of_the_review: My main concern about this work is that it's not doing very well on MNLI, and that we don't know how to improve its performance at inference time while the baseline allows trading-off compute with accuracy. Therefore, I'm not recommending the acceptance of this work in its current form.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

display_title: Faithfulness, Efficiency-Stability Trade-off, and Ranking-based Method

content.title: Faithfulness, Efficiency-Stability Trade-off, and Ranking-based Method
content.comment:
Thanks for the thoughtful comments from the reviewer. We reply to each concern in detail below:

**Regarding the faithfulness problem**: 

Thanks for bringing out the concern. Regarding our model performance on the MNLI dataset, as we show in the learning curve in Figure 3, our model has the potential to achieve higher spearman correlation had we kept training on more data. We are restricted by the data size because we use the pre-collected Shapley Values from Thermostat as the training data, and the dataset size of Thermostat-MNLI is much less than that of Yelp-Polarity.  

We agree faithfulness is an important aspect when evaluating model explanations. However, we see there are arguably different definitions for faithfulness, and there are no universally agreed metrics [1]. Although the spearman correlation of our model on the MNLI dataset is not very satisfying, in Section 6.4, we do show that explanation scores generated by our models can help calibrate the model to the new domain using the method proposed by [2], and it works better than KernelSHAP-2000. As [2] discussed in their paper, this means the explanation generated by our model is better associated with how the model would work to solve the task (one possible definition of “faithfulness”).  The usage of the downstream task to evaluate the quality of explanations is also recommended as “a functionality evaluation of model interpretation” in the widely-recognized paper [3] on explanation evaluation.

**Regarding efficiency-stability trade-off and guided importance sampling**: 

Good point! In the revision of the paper, we show that by using our model output as an initialization, we can achieve a higher correlation by running an SVS update on very few perturbation samples (e.g., on MNLI, we can actually achieve 0.57 Spearman’s correlation by only using five perturbation samples). Details are in revision (Section 5 and Appendix B).

**Regarding the ranking-based method**: 

Thanks for raising this concern! We actually have run a simple adaptation of the state-of-the-art ranking method, sorting network [4], which helps the model learn to rank by continuous relaxation. But it turns out this simple learning-to-rank adaptation is hard to optimize in practice, and we cannot achieve better results compared with simple L2 regression.  We discuss more technical details in the revision (Section 5). 

References:

[1] Lyu, Qing, Marianna Apidianaki, and Chris Callison-Burch. "Towards Faithful Model Explanation in NLP: A Survey." arXiv preprint arXiv:2209.11326 (2022).

[2] Ye, Xi, and Greg Durrett. "Can Explanations Be Useful for Calibrating Black Box Models?." ACL 2022.

[3] Doshi-Velez, Finale, and Been Kim. "Towards a rigorous science of interpretable machine learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1702.08608 (2017).

[4] Petersen, Felix, et al. "Monotonic Differentiable Sorting Networks." ICLR 2021.

display_title: Analysis, Technical Depth and Related Works

content.title: Analysis, Technical Depth and Related Works
content.comment:
Thanks for the thoughtful comments from the reviewer. We reply to each concern in detail below :

**Regarding theoretic intrinsic effects analysis for unstable explanation**: 

Good question.  While we do not have strong theoretical conclusions about why such an instability problem occurs, we have some hypotheses. We believe it is because, in the text domain, the tasks usually require models to perform high-level correlation analysis among many tokens beyond 2-gram, and missing even one token can drastically change the semantics of the input. Furthermore, when the input length grows, the number of n-grams will grow fast, roughly at the speed of O(L^n). But as we have seen in Section 3, in Shapley Values, the probability of each n-gram getting sampled is equivalent for all n-grams. Therefore, the probability of certain n-grams getting sampled will drastically reduce, which can lead to suboptimal explanation results [1]. We have added this discussion in Section 4. Note that Figure 2 also demonstrates that the stability will reduce as the input length goes up. 

**Regarding the depth of the technique**:

For Shapley Value and KernelSHAP, we choose them as they are particularly popular and representative of black-box explanation methods in NLP. We are building an amortized model to efficiently and stably estimate the values using pre-collected Shapley Value and KernelSHAP values. As our method does not assume details of Shapley Value and KernelSHAP, our method is generally applicable to another improvement of other Shapley Value variants. 

Actually, in our revised draft, we further show two additional modeling designs: 

1) we can utilize the amortized model output as a good initialization for performing an SVS update on each test instance to achieve a better fit for expensive full Shapley Value computation (see the updated section 5 and Appendix B);

2) we also experiment with a ranking-based method using the state-of-the-art sorting network method [2], but it turns out a straightforward application of this method will make training pretty unstable. We hypothesize it might be due to the discrete nature of the text, making it hard to learn to sort. We briefly discuss our experiment results at the end of section 5, marked with a green change bar. 
We leave more exploration for model variants for future work.

**Regarding why random seeds matter**: 

Thanks for raising this concern! In Shapley Value and KernelSHAP, the random seeds matter as they will influence the perturbation sampling process we use to compute these values.  Different random seeds will result in a set of different perturbation samples used in further Shapley Value / KernelSHAP computation. We updated the paper in section 3. 

**Related Works are not enough**: 

Thanks for pointing that out. We have reviewed more works and updated Section 2 in the revised version. 
Baseline not convincing: Thanks for suggesting related works in the time series domain. We will discuss related explanation methods in the time series domain as well. For baseline setting, to the best of our knowledge, FastSHAP is the first and the most recent work that proposes to build amortized models for generating Shapley Values explanation, although not originally applied to text data. We adapt FastSHAP methods (we describe how to do it in Appendix A) on text data to make a convincing baseline. 

**Experiment analysis not enough**: 

We have carefully revised our experiment analysis and made edits to Section 4 to discuss why Shapley Values computation can be insatiable in the text domain and why longer inputs suffer more. 

> Can properly back up the claims with evidence somewhere for “As a result, a much larger number of model evaluations is needed to reduce the sensitivity to an acceptable level.”?

We discuss this sensitivity analysis in section 4. Specifically, we refer the reviewer to Table 1 and Table 2. You can see that only after doing >2000 model queries (KernelSHAP-2000 means we will do 2000 model evaluations to compute KernelSHAP values), self-correlation (in terms of Spearman) can reach an acceptable level (strong correlation, >0.6). We have updated the paper to make it more clear in section 4, immediately following the analysis “trade-off between stability and computation cost.”

**Reference fix**: 

Thanks for the suggestions. We have cleaned the paper references in the revision.  

[1] Kwon, Yongchan, and James Zou. "WeightedSHAP: analyzing and improving Shapley based feature attributions." NeurIPS 2022. 

[2] Petersen, Felix, et al. "Monotonic Differentiable Sorting Networks." ICLR 2021.

display_title: Trustworthy Evaluation of Explanation and Generalization across Datasets

content.title: Trustworthy Evaluation of Explanation and Generalization across Datasets
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the detailed and insightful comments. 

**About Trustworthy Evaluation of Explanation**: 

In the literature, there are various ways to evaluate whether the explanation is trustworthy. In this paper, we take a functionality perspective to evaluate the quality of explanations generated by our amortized model (i.e., whether the explanation can be helpful for downstream tasks such as feature selection and calibration). This follows the recommended practice of this widely-recognized "rigorous science of evaluating interpretation" paper [1]. 

**About Generalizable Performance**: 

We are not clear about the meaning of “generalizable” here. We have two interpretations of this comment here: 

1) The reviewer is talking about the amortized explanation model as dataset-specific and cannot be transferred to other datasets. Actually, the transferability problem is a long-existing problem for computing explanation scores. Explanation scores are often computed per instance, and they cannot transfer across instances or even across datasets. Because different datasets may have significant distribution shifts.  Practitioners often train separate models for each dataset to obtain the overall best performance and produce explanation scores for each model on each instance. As we will work with different models, it is reasonable to have model-specific explanations for each model.


2) The reviewer is talking about why in MNLI, our model performance is not good as on Yelp, as also pointed out by reviewer RHYE. Regarding this problem, we refer to our learning curve (Figure 2) for MNLI. From that figure, we can see it is very likely that the potential for the amortized model has not been fulfilled yet. Unfortunately, the existing thermostat dataset for MNLI is not large enough, and it is pretty expensive (in time and budget) to collect more samples for training. Still, our simple method wins the previous method, FastSHAP, by a large margin. And on downstream tasks, it turns out to be a good and stable substitute for expensive KernelSHAP methods (unless using more than 2000 perturbation samples, which is overly expensive in the NLP domain as we need to query large language models 2000 times).  We leave a more sample-efficient amortized model building for future work.

[1] Doshi-Velez, Finale, and Been Kim. "Towards a rigorous science of interpretable machine learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1702.08608 (2017).

content.title: About generalisability
content.comment:
Hi, thanks for the explanation. I am talking about the first problem. 

When a fixed model trained on dataset A is applied to an example B, which is an example of interest for imterpretability methods, the Shapley value will provide insightful explanations for how the model performs. However, the proposed method will have a larger bias than being applied to examples from dataset A because it was trained on dataset A as well. 

Because of this increased bias (without any guarantee), people will hesitate about using the method in practice for such settings.

More severely, this problem introduced a bias when applied to training and test examples of the same dataset!

content.title: Explanation on out-of-distribution data
content.comment:
Thanks for the clarification! 

Your observation is correct that our amortized model can be biased on out-of-distribution (OOD) data. To see how well our model can perform on OOD data, we did the following experiments. We trained a classification model on Yelp-Polarity and then explained its performance on SST-2 validation set. Both tasks are two-way sentiment classification and have significant domain differences. We find that our amortized model can achieve about 0.50 spearman correlation with ground truth Shapley Values (SVS-25) and only requires 0.017s per instance. In comparison, KernelSHAP-100 can only achieve 0.46 spearman with ground truth SVS-25 and needs 1.6s per instance (KernelSHAP-200 can only achieve a slightly better spearman but needs much more time), which is more than 90 times slower and less correlated with ground truth Shapley Values. So once our amortized model is trained, it can give a reasonably good, efficient, and stable Shapley Values estimation even on OOD data. We will add this discussion in the final version. In Appendix B of the current version, we also present a meta-learning-based method to mitigate OOD bias. 

It is common for estimators to trade off bias for other desired merits, such as better efficiency and lower variances. In our work, we build an amortized model to estimate Shapley Values, which achieves a much better efficiency-stability trade-off than widely-used sampling-based methods (SVS and KernelSHAP) in our experiments. 

Furthermore, in practice, it seems not recommended to explain model predictions on OOD data because it may be socially misaligned with users’ expectations for explanations, or the OOD explanations are not reliable to trust [1, 2]. More exploration on this side is interesting, but is orthogonal to our works. 

References:

[1] Hase, Peter, Harry Xie, and Mohit Bansal. "The out-of-distribution problem in explainability and search methods for feature importance explanations." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 3650-3666.

[2] Denain, Jean-Stanislas, and Jacob Steinhardt. "Auditing Visualizations: Transparency Methods Struggle to Detect Anomalous Behavior." arXiv preprint arXiv:2206.13498 (2022).
